title: Coupled Equilibria
lead: A sparingly soluble salt can share an ion with a second equilibrium, an acid-base reaction or the formation of a complex ion, so that the two equilibria shift together. Coral reefs, tooth enamel, and aluminum hydroxide in acid and in base show what such coupling does to solubility.
objectives: Describe examples of systems involving two (or more) coupled chemical equilibria
Calculate reactant and product concentrations for coupled equilibrium systems
summary_html: Systems involving two or more chemical equilibria that share one or more reactant or product are called coupled equilibria. Common examples of coupled equilibria include the increased solubility of some compounds in acidic solutions (coupled dissolution and neutralization equilibria) and in solutions containing ligands (coupled dissolution and complex formation). The equilibrium tools from other chapters may be applied to describe and perform calculations on these systems.

exercises.prompt: What is the solubility of aluminum hydroxide in a buffer comprised of 0.100 M formic acid and 0.100 M sodium formate?

answer.hint: Find the pH of the buffer from the pKa of formic acid with the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation, then [OH−], then [Al3+] from Ksp, as in Example 15.15.

exercises.prompt: AgCl(s), silver chloride, has a very low solubility: $\text{AgCl}(s)\rightleftharpoons {\text{Ag}}^{\text{+}}(aq)+{\text{Cl}}^{\text{−}}(aq),$ Ksp = 1.6 × 10–10. Adding ammonia significantly increases the solubility of AgCl because a complex ion is formed: ${\text{Ag}}^{\text{+}}(aq)+2{\text{NH}}_{3}(aq)\rightleftharpoons \text{Ag}{({\text{NH}}_{3})}_{2}{}^{+}(aq),$ Kf = 1.7 × 107. What mass of NH3 is required to prepare 1.00 L of solution that will dissolve 2.00 g of AgCl by formation of $\text{Ag}{({\text{NH}}_{3})}_{2}{}^{\text{+}}?$

answer.hint: Combine the two equilibria into one with K = KspKf, find the free [NH3] it leaves, and add the ammonia bound in the complex, as in Example 15.16.
answer.solution: 1.00 L of a solution prepared with 5.0 g NH<sub>3</sub> dissolves 2.0 g of AgCl.

exercises.prompt: Explain why the addition of NH<sub>3</sub> or HNO<sub>3</sub> to a saturated solution of Ag<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> in contact with solid Ag<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> increases the solubility of the solid.

answer.solution: Suggested approach: write the dissolution equilibrium of Ag<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>, then couple it in turn with the formation of the complex ion Ag(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> and with the reaction of carbonate ion, a base, with the hydronium ion of the acid. Say which ion each added substance removes from the solution and which way that shifts the dissolution equilibrium.

exercises.prompt: Explain why addition of NH<sub>3</sub> or HNO<sub>3</sub> to a saturated solution of Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub> in contact with solid Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub> increases the solubility of the solid.

answer.solution: Suggested approach: write the dissolution equilibrium of Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub>, then couple it in turn with the formation of a complex ion of Cu<sup>2+</sup> with ammonia and with the neutralization of hydroxide ion by the acid. Say which ion each added substance removes from the solution and which way that shifts the dissolution equilibrium.

exercises.prompt: Calculate the molar solubility of Al(OH)3 in a buffer solution with 0.100 M NH3 and 0.400 M ${\text{NH}}_{4}{}^{+}.$

parts.hint: Find the hydroxide ion concentration of the buffer from Kb of ammonia and the ratio of the two concentrations.
Divide Ksp by the cube of [OH−], as in Example 15.15.

exercises.prompt: What is the molar solubility of BaSO4 in a 0.250-M solution of NaHSO4? Ka for ${\text{HSO}}_{4}{}^{\text{−}}$ = 1.2 × 10–2.

answer.hint: Find [SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>] from the ionization of HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> first; it is a common ion for the dissolution of BaSO<sub>4</sub>.

exercises.prompt: What is the molar solubility of Pb(OH)2 in a 0.138-M solution of CH3NH2?

parts.hint: Find the hydroxide ion concentration from the base ionization of methylamine first.
Divide Ksp of Pb(OH)2 by the square of [OH−].

exercises.prompt:
A 0.125-M solution of Mn(NO3)2 is saturated with H2S ([H2S] = 0.10 M). At what pH does MnS begin to precipitate?
$\text{MnS}(s)\rightleftharpoons {\text{Mn}}^{\text{2+}}(aq)+{\text{S}}^{\text{2−}}(aq)\hspace{4em}{K}_{\text{sp}}=2.3\;\times \;{10}^{\text{−13}}$
${\text{H}}_{2}\text{S}(aq)+2{\text{H}}_{2}\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons 2{\text{H}}_{3}{\text{O}}^{\text{+}}(aq)+{\text{S}}^{\text{2−}}(aq)\hspace{4em}K=1.0\;\times \;{10}^{\text{−26}}$

answer.hint: Find the [S2−] at which the ion product of MnS reaches Ksp, then the [H3O+] that the H2S equilibrium allows at that [S2−].

exercises.prompt: Which of the following compounds, when dissolved in a 0.01-M solution of HClO4, has a solubility greater than in pure water: CuCl, CaCO3, MnS, PbBr2, CaF2? Explain your answer.

answer.solution: Suggested approach: for each salt, decide whether its anion is the conjugate base of a weak acid or of a strong acid. Hydronium ion from the HClO<sub>4</sub> removes a basic anion from the solution and pulls the dissolution equilibrium to the right, as it does for calcium carbonate in this section; an anion of a strong acid is left as it is.

exercises.prompt: Which of the following compounds, when dissolved in a 0.01-M solution of HClO4, has a solubility greater than in pure water: AgBr, BaF2, Ca3(PO4)2, ZnS, PbI2? Explain your answer.

answer.solution: BaF<sub>2</sub>, Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, ZnS; each is a salt of a weak acid, and the $[{\text{H}}_{3}{\text{O}}^{+}]$ from perchloric acid reduces the equilibrium concentration of the anion, thereby increasing the concentration of the cations

exercises.prompt:
What is the effect on the amount of solid Mg(OH)2 that dissolves and the concentrations of Mg2+ and OH– when each of the following are added to a mixture of solid Mg(OH)2 and water at equilibrium?
(a) MgCl2
(b) KOH
(c) HClO4
(d) NaNO3
(e) Mg(OH)2

answer.solution: Suggested approach: write the dissolution equilibrium of Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub>. For each added substance, decide whether it adds Mg<sup>2+</sup> or OH<sup>–</sup> as a common ion, removes OH<sup>–</sup> by neutralization, or takes part in neither reaction, and apply Le Châtelier’s principle to the amount of solid and to each concentration. Remember that adding more of a solid does not change the concentrations of a saturated solution.

exercises.prompt:
What is the effect on the amount of CaHPO4 that dissolves and the concentrations of Ca2+ and ${\text{HPO}}_{4}{}^{\text{2−}}$ when each of the following are added to a mixture of solid CaHPO4 and water at equilibrium?
(a) CaCl2
(b) HCl
(c) KClO4
(d) NaOH
(e) CaHPO4

answer.solution: Effect on amount of solid CaHPO<sub>4</sub>, [Ca<sup>2+</sup>], [OH<sup>–</sup>]: (a) increase, increase, decrease; (b) decrease, increase, decrease; (c) no effect, no effect, no effect; (d) decrease, increase, decrease; (e) increase, no effect, no effect

exercises.prompt: Identify all chemical species present in an aqueous solution of Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub> and list these species in decreasing order of their concentrations. (Hint: Remember that the ${\text{PO}}_{4}{}^{\text{3−}}$ ion is a weak base.)

answer.solution: Suggested approach: write the dissolution equilibrium of Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub> and then the stepwise reactions of PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup> with water as a base, each step much less extensive than the one before, as for a polyprotic base. Include water itself and the ions it forms, and rank the species by how much of each the small solubility product and the successive steps leave.
